newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. plane to check possible NKorea missile launch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plane to check possible NKorea missile launch.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday sent an advanced reconnaissance plane to monitor the possible imminent test firing by North Korea of a medium-range ballistic missile into seas just off the Japanese coast.
A U.S. military spokesman in Tokyo told Reuters the modified C-135 aircraft was on station in the area to feed back information of any firing.
He said the high-altitude plane with the most up-to-date reconnaissance equipment was sent from the U.S. military base at Kadena in Japan's southernmost island of Okinawa.

An official from Japan's Self Defence Agency (SDF) told Kyodo news service a U.S. reconnaissance satellite had confirmed that North Korea had moved a launch platform for the Rodong-1 missile, capable of reaching a large part of Japan, out of the missile's assembly plant in eastern North Korea.
The Rodong 1, with a range of about 1,000 kilometres (600 miles), is based on the Soviet Scud design used by Iraq in the Gulf War.
The official said North Korean observation ships were already at the scene of the missile's target area in the Sea of Japan, Kyodo reported.
Kyodo said Pyongyang has given no warning of an imminent missile launch, and neither U.S. nor Japanese defence officials are sure if the preparations in North Korea will lead to an actual test.
Japanese Defence Agency officials say there were signs of North Korean preparations to test-fire a Rodong-1 missile in July but at that time there was no actual launch.

"Some defence observers suggest that the North Korean government may just be feigning a missile launch. Pyongyang has hinted of taking action against South Korea in retaliation for the South's handling of the North Korean submarine that ran aground on South Korea's eastern coast last month," Kyodo said.
Last week the London-based think tank, International Institute for Strategic Studies, said North Korea was likely to deploy Rodong-1 missiles later this year or early next year.

The London-based think tank also said North Korea was developing two longer-range missiles -- the Taepodong-1 with a range of 1,500 km (900 miles) and Taepodong-2 with a range of 4,000 km (2,400 miles).

Japan's Jiji news agency said a military delegation from the Middle East, apparently from Iran, was also at the launching site, and that North Korea planned the test-firing as part of a demonstration aimed at selling missiles to Iran.
In May 1993, North Korea shocked Japan by test-firing its Rodong-1 ballistic missile into waters just off the coast of the Noto peninsula in the Sea of Japan.
U.S. spy satellites caught the launch and tracked its trajectory, but Japan was caught off guard.
The U.S. Air Force C-135 reconnaissance plane sent to the area has a crew of about 25 and was used extensively as an airborne command base during the Gulf War.
